utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you so much, and again once more good morning to you. Prosecution and Defence, we decided yesterday, since there are too many of you - too many accused, too many Defence counsel - and a usually constant appearance, that we'll try and freshen up a little bit the procedure. Instead of going through each one of the accused and then each one of the Defence, Prosecution, what we will do is I will just put one single question, asking the accused if any of them are not able to follow the proceedings in a language that they understand, to stand up now and at any time later on during the proceedings if it's the case of not receiving interpretation. So I take it that you all are. And then I will not be asking for appearances but you are expected from day to day that, if there are any changes in the composition of your respective teams, to stand up and make the relative announcement. Agreed? Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, you've been abandoned by Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, they are, of course, busy with the next two witnesses, but Lada Soljan is here today, and I will try to be here as much as I can unless I'm with a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Your cooperation is much appreciated, Mr. McCloskey. So I understand there is a statement you would like to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just very briefly. I discussed this with most counsel yesterday. I know everyone has been reading in the press about a new potential mass grave from Srebrenica, allegedly the largest mass grave found, over a thousand bodies. We looked into this and there appears to have been a mass grave that has been found. It does not have a thousand bodies. It appears to be what looks like the normal secondary grave and has probably 140 or 150 bodies and many, many body parts. So information of this sort, as you can imagine, is very emotional and sometimes prone to exaggeration. So I just wanted to get that out. We will get more details on that, but I believe it is a secondary mass grave, it may very well be one that is already incorporated into our evidence, and if not, we'll -- we will incorporate it. But we'll have better information on that for you in the future, but I did not want anyone to think that there was another grave with over a thousand bodies out there. That is not the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I also understand that the Prosecution agrees with the way shown or indicated as the Defence of -- Defence preference for the presentation or availability of cross-examination documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So we'll be proceeding with later on in the day, hopefully, with the relative decision, which will be along the same lines indicated in the Milosevic -- in the Milutinovic decision. Last but not least, Madam Nikolic in particular, I'm sure you are aware of the latest filing by the Prosecution in relation to tomorrow's witness. And I suppose you have no special comments to make because it more or less answers the concern that you expressed yesterday or the day before. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any one of the Defence teams that would like to address the subject matter of this latest Prosecution filing, details of which I'm not going into because of the confidentiality of the motion. Okay. Thank you. Again, please expect a decision on those protective measures later on in the day today. Yes. Mr. Ostojic, good morning to you. You have the floor, and also the lectern.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Yesterday we left off discussing several topics which we think are relevant and important to ultimately adjudicating the case as it relates to Mr. Beara. We spoke briefly about collective guilt and how the Madam Prosecutor herself Monday told us that it is not about collective guilt. In our opinion it's easy to say something is not this and yet try to prove your case through what we call the side or the back door. The Prosecution, I think, tells us they don't believe in collective guilt but continues to lump the accused and continues to argue down the road of collective guilt. Collective guilt, in our view, is nothing other than if you argue that specific intent follows you into your job. Genocide, as it is in this jurisprudence, does not subscribe to that view or that position. Specific intent doesn't follow you into a job. We'll see that that's the view of the Prosecution, and we hope that the Court recognises that all it is is a substitution of a few words to actually talk about collective guilt which they themselves reject and they themselves acknowledge is not part of the jurisprudence in this case. Yesterday we spoke a little bit about Mr. Beara and his rank and how it maintained the same since 1995 -- 1985. I'd like today to begin, if I may, with the theory called tried and tested. Mr. Beara's case and the allegations against Mr. Beara -- [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. -- have, in our view, been tried and tested on at least two different occasions. The first occasion was during the Krstic trial when the Defence of General Krstic and his Defence lawyers actually advocated an empty chair Defence. In essence, in my jurisdiction that is where they shift or try to shift the blame and responsibility to an accused who is not present. Any facts from that case which can be seen to be adverse to Mr. Beara should be looked at that he didn't have a right to cross-examine, didn't have a right to confront his witnesses, and obviously had lost his presumption of innocence since he was not present. However, despite those three rights that Mr. Beara has, the Prosecution in that case tirelessly and steadfastly argued against this theory called dual functional relationship where the Defence there tried to shift the blame on the security officers and shift the blame on the staff officer of the security unit, namely Mr. Beara. The Prosecution was successful and convinced the Court, and rightfully so, that it was not the security staff officer who was responsible or culpable but General Krstic. That same theory was subsequently examined in the Appellate Court and the Appellate Court again rightfully found that it was not Mr. Beara, it was General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for objecting, but that is just not a fact. Neither the Prosecution view nor the Appellate Court's view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to expand, if I may, on that, Your Honour. And if we look -- if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, but please be precise, because I think what Mr. McCloskey has objected, having read both decisions myself, and I will assume also my colleagues, you're not being precise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe that I am precise, with all due respect to the Prosecutor. If we look at the second time the case was tried and tested, it was tried and tested in the Blagojevic case where specifically, specifically witnesses were brought in by the Defence attorney, not by Mr. Blagojevic - because we know that history - they were brought in and they shifted the blame, or tried to shift the blame on Mr. Beara. Specifically those witnesses testified. They have now become ultimately and all of a sudden witnesses for the Prosecution. We'll talk a little bit about those witnesses in a few minutes. However in that same case, I submit respectfully to Your Honours, that the Court rejected that dual functional relationship where there is a parallel hierarchy or a parallel chain, rejected it. They found Mr. Blagojevic guilty. I'd like to inform the Court that I dare say that Mr. Beara can hold a candle to Mr. Blagojevic -- that he cannot hold a handle to Mr. Blagojevic. The evidence will show that Mr. Beara was a mere staff officer in the security unit, did not perpetrate, participate, or commit any of the crimes against them. We spoke a little bit about integrity and if -- I'm going to play a tape, with the Court's permission, if I may, and it's merely a five-minute tape, and just by way of background - I'm going to explain it - when we talk about integrity, I was proud of my colleague at the Prosecution's office when he said that integrity is not a laughing matter and I don't want someone to poke fun at my integrity or to make a joke of my integrity. And then we proceed -- that's the first section of the tape, which is about 30 seconds. I believe Your Honour is on it as well. The second section of the tape is from the September closing argument of Blagojevic. And I ask this Court to specifically listen carefully to the comments of the Prosecution yesterday - meaning in the Blagojevic trial - and today. It's a four-minute tape, and I would like to play it especially in light of the objection that we just heard moments ago. So would the gentlemen in the video booth please play the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a rather novel approach, and I would object to this. I think we all -- the idea that my comments earlier in this trial are somehow relevant to an opening statement is -- I don't think it is. I think, having just not been able to give it much thought, but we need to, in this trial, be able to speak freely and not think that our comments are going to be televised again. I don't mind my comments being televised. He can televise my entire closing statement in the Blagojevic case, but I don't see the relevance of it and it -- nor the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't let the fact that we are going to see a first section referring to your statement disturb you that much, because I wouldn't worry about it. But on the other hand, I think the whole purpose of this exercise is to put this in juxtaposition with what you stated in your opening statement in this case, contrasting it with what -- if I have understood Mr. Ostojic well, contrasting it with what was the Prosecution's position in Blagojevic. Let's go through it first, and if it's not regular, then of course we'll stop it or reverse our decision, but for the time being I think we should listen or look at what is being proposed by Mr. Ostojic. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Understood. And on the point of discussing what the Prosecution's position was and what the Court did in Blagojevic, we are very proud of what we did, and I know the decision of the Court was very carefully thought out, and we have used the law as we felt it allowed us to under judicial notice and adjudicated facts to bring that material to your attention. However, many of the conclusions and legal conclusions and theories of the Court, the law does not allow us to bring forward to you and we have not. That would be extremely prejudicial to many of these accused. And -- however, if this door becomes open, that it may be it would then become relevant. I don't want to re-argue that case again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see after we've gone through these two videos or whatever they are. And if it's necessary to give you the floor, Mr. McCloskey, we certainly will. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Would the gentlemen in the video booth please play the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: "JUDGE AGIUS: ... Mr. McCloskey and then we will see. If we have reason to be strict with the Prosecutor, then we will do so. "MS. CONDON: I won't make any comment about trusting prosecutors, Your Honour. "JUDGE AGIUS: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, any comment on that?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm only receiving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "JUDGE AGIUS: Mr. Ostojic -- "MR. McCLOSKEY: I would prefer her to come by me before she makes statements. And statements that are going to go to my integrity, I don't appreciate jokes either. "JUDGE AGIUS: Okay. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Ostojic --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic, I repeat--

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It continues to play, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to see more?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the second portion, Your Honour, is playing now. If we can just start it again at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: "... command chain, I say third man, it's Mladic, Krstic, Blagojevic. That's the way it is. Two generals and a colonel. We've got the MUP and we've got others. These are the commanders. These are the key guys. Now, we have Beara, we have Popovic, we have Nikolic, we have Drago Nikolic. These guys are staff officers. One of the reasons they get charged with genocide is because staff officers in the security branch have chosen to be in the security branch and it's an ugly job and if you're chosen to be in that job, specific intent is a -- follows you into that job, in the view of the Prosecution. But they are staff officers. Colonel Beara can't hold a candle to Colonel Blagojevic. Colonel Beara -- and we've made this very clear because we do not want to suggest Dragan Jokic is a commander because there is a huge difference, a huge difference. A staff officer is an empty vessel and only has the power that is given to him by his commander. Beara is nothing but a sicko, an empty vessel, until Mladic gives him those orders. He doesn't have the right to command troops, he doesn't have any troops, the same thing with Popovic. "These guys -- and I don't know how to communicate this to you, but in a -- in the military context they don't even go to the same function as the commanders do. They don't have the power, the authority and you can see it. And I'll -- if I get time, I'll point you out some of the examples. But you need to understand that. It's the commanders are the ones that call the shots. They're the ones that can make the difference, they're are the ones that have the men. And especially in the brigades. Remember, the Main Staff has a Protection Regiment and 10th Diversionary Unit. The Protection Regiment's designed to protect Han Pijesak and other areas. The Sabotage Detachment is a sabotage mission to go in. They don't really have very many troops. The brigade is even -- or the corps is even less. They have a small MP squad. They've got, you know, the 5th Engineers, they have a couple of other units that aren't really involved here. It's the brigade. The brigade has -- he's got over 2.000 men under arms. He knows where the fuel is, he knows where the logistics bases are. This is their home base. "The brigade commanders are the key players in this and he's a colonel. I can't overstate that, that principle, how important the brigade guys are. The brigade guys are the guys that are dying in the trenches. And it's the Blagojevics of that war that are there to protect them and their town, to give it in a positive sense. Not the Krstics and the Mladics and the others. So a commander with honour is the man that takes the blame when things are bad and gets the blame when things are good. When war crimes go down, they have to take it the same way. They can't just put it on the evil staff officers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe it stops there. Thank you, Your Honour. There are a couple of points in our opening statement we would like to at least address with respect to the comments made in the last two days and, I think, in other cases. There are more, obviously, and we don't want to waste our time by splicing them and showing them to the Court, but I think it's important when we talk, on Monday or last month, about integrity and when we talk about presenting to the Court certain things, that we maintain that honour and that we continue to tell the Court, yes, we are offended when someone attacks our credibility, our integrity and our reputation, but we must also work, in my view, hard to maintain that level of trust. I promise this Court that what I say in my opening statement with respect to Mr. Beara, we will bring forth the evidence regarding the September -- the 1992 incident. We will bring the Prosecutor, hopefully, and/or the Judge. Similarly, we'll bring in the articles and explain to the Court the September 1993. However, I believe that the same standard should be held to the Prosecutor and even more so, and that is because they carry the burden of proof. And that burden of proof should not -- and their theory of the case should not change from day to day, from witness to witness. Our client, Mr. Beara, is entitled to a trial on his own, on his own merits, not because of the joinder but because the facts as they stay. The Prosecutor cannot in one courtroom suggest, in our view, that someone else is to blame and come in this courtroom and tell us that another person is to blame. He himself, we believe, and the evidence will show, that you cannot blame the evil staff officers. Why he believes they are evil, hopefully he'll bring forth that evidence. We believe that you cannot blame the staff officers. We believe that there is no evidence for there to be blame attributed to the staff officers. Also, the Prosecutor suggests that the orders may flow down. There is no such thing in any criminal jurisprudence or any military army that a nod or a wink authorises someone to carry forth orders. The Prosecutor a couple years ago suggested that Mladic gave an order to Mr. Beara. Where is the evidence? Did we see it yesterday? Did he present it in his binder for Mr. Beara? No. Trust me on this: There is no evidence that General Mladic gave Mr. Beara orders to kill or to transfer any of the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica in 1995. Their best witness, who will come here, has a slightly different version, again depending on the day that he testifies, as to purportedly who may have given Mr. Beara some instructions. We hope that you'll find this witness, or as he comes -- although Mr. McCloskey calls some of his own witnesses, I think he used the word "bald faced liars" -- we hope that you'll find this witness's testimony less than credible, and I believe that it is not believable, and we'll get into that a little later. Tried and tested? I honestly believe it has been. The Prosecutor could have easily said that we believe whatever the Defence says in those cases, they may be correct, but we have enough evidence out of Blagojevic. They chose not to. They chose to tell the Court what their theory of genocide is specifically when they mentioned specific intent relating to the staff officers in the security unit. They said it flows with the job. Mr. Beara was a staff officer and Mr. Beara was working as a security in the security unit ten years, at the very least, prior to Srebrenica. Did it follow him in 1985? It does not hold water that they can suggest other than, with one exception, and that's the exception that the Madam Prosecutor told us she will not, because it does not exist, and that is collective guilt. So our view is you must look at the evidence specifically for Mr. Beara, take what they've done, and they've worked on this case for well over eight years, now ten, they've examined all the facts, the documents, the intercepts, the witnesses, and two years ago they tell this Honourable Court - not specifically Your Honours but an Honourable Court at this Tribunal - that it flows, specific intent flows to people. We suggest that the evidence will show that it does not flow, and we suggest that they cannot meet their burden of proof, and we suggest that there was no specific intent as it relates to Mr. Beara at any time relating all the incidents, all the tragedy, all the massacres that occurred in Srebrenica in 1995. Tried and tested. We'll hear from many witnesses who have testified who have been cross-examined, who have been put on redirect, given multiple witness statements; all this has been done, and I've tried to give you a snippet of what the Prosecution's theory really is against these mere staff officers. I challenged them, as I expect to be challenged, that when they say General Mladic gave an order, that they can prove it. It's not my job to tell this Court that he didn't or to prove somehow - by calling him? It's their job then to tell the Court when we made that comment it's erroneous or we don't have the proof to substantiate that claim. There is no witness, there is no intercept, there is no document to suggest, infer, much less determine or establish, that General Mladic gave Mr. Beara any orders, specifically orders to kill or to massacre. It just doesn't exist. He says that Mr. Beara cannot hold a candle to Colonel Blagojevic. His words. Although I used them before I played the tape, those are his words. That should remain true if we have integrity and honesty throughout the process, not to pick and choose and to elevate an accused but it should be maintained throughout the entire process. That's what integrity is. That's what character is, in my view. And that's what we hope to establish for the Court throughout these proceedings. We will not, unfortunately, be able to share this with the Court early in the trial because it is a lengthy trial. We know that the Court will continue to maintain objectivity and wait until all the evidence is in before you render a decision, and I say it most respectfully, but it may be difficult when someone continues to press forward with a theory that we believe may be inadequate, improper, unsubstantiated by law, and wait a year for us to come back and try to rebut or refute or contradict that theory. Therefore we chose to give an opening statement this time in order just not to let a year pass by, in order to address these very concrete issues up front with the Court. We will, in our case, hopefully specifically not only contradict but rebut the evidence that the Prosecution claims to have against Mr. Beara. My next section that I would like to discuss with Your Honours is something that Madam Prosecutor said on Monday, and she is right. Strike that. She is right, but she said it July 14th of this year. I'm not sure if it was taken in the transcripts but I heard it, and I don't think it's necessary to check the transcript for this: She, when we objected to her giving her statement, part of her opening statement, she stood up and said, "Facts, just facts." It's a great phrase: Facts, just facts. I've listened to her opening statement on Monday. I've heard conclusions. She concluded that there was genocide. She concluded who was mostly culpable in her view. The Prosecutor likewise leapt to conclusions, in our view. Those weren't facts. Those were conclusions. Your Honours, respectfully, will come up with the conclusions only after we provide you with the necessary facts so that you may be fully informed, and that's our job, and I promise you that we will give you the facts which, in our view, will exonerate Mr. Beara. What are those facts, just facts? We touched upon a few of them yesterday, late in the afternoon. We believe that if the Court respectfully looks at those facts properly, objectively, and honestly, Mr. Beara will be found not guilty. Those facts, some are not in dispute. Some may not be in dispute. And yet, others are. What are those facts? That he was not only a staff officer but, in the words of the Prosecution, merely a staff officer. Mr. Beara. That's a critical fact. That Mr. Beara had no military personnel to control, direct or command. That also is a fact that cannot be rebutted or contradicted. That Ljubisa Beara was not a member of "an inner circle." The word "inner circle" I believe was coined by the Prosecutor in their pre-trial brief, and if Your Honours would like, I could get you the page specifically. I'm confident that it's in there. It's significant to say that Mr. Beara was not a member of an inner circle because the Prosecution alleges there are participants in this inner circle. Separate trial for Mr. Beara? He is not a member of the inner circle. By their silence - not now, of course, but in their brief - by not saying Mr. Beara was in this inner circle they are clearly telling us he was not a member of the inner circle. Yesterday I discussed to you about Mr. Beara's promotion. I failed to mention it's not just a promotion from his rank of colonel, or before that when he was a navy captain in a battleship prior to 1985, but it is in fact -- he was never decorated, never awarded medals. That's relevant. That's relevant to the theory of the Defence and the facts in this case which are undisputed to show his detachment, to show his isolation, if you will, during the events of Srebrenica in 1995. Mr. Beara did not have the authority to command or to direct subordinate military troops or personnel. Mr. Beara did not have the power to command or direct military personnel subordinate or otherwise. Another critical fact: We saw pictures; we are going to see, I'm confident, videos. Did Mr. Beara participate in what the Prosecution will try to share with you are important or relevant meetings? The evidence will show quite plainly, quite objectively, quite unanimously, he did not participate in any relevant or important meetings. He did not attend, nor was he invited to any such important meetings. You might be wondering, although you may know, respectfully, what are some of those meetings? Well, the Prosecutor touched on it a little bit yesterday. The Hotel Fontana meeting on July 11 and 12 of 1995. Those are facts. When we look at those videos, with respect to Mr. Beara, he was not present, he did not participate, there was never an invitation, and there is no evidence to suggest that he was informed of the contents of the meetings that occurred. Three meetings, not one. The other discussion - I believe the Prosecutor touched on it - there was a meeting immediately prior to the third meeting at the Hotel Fontana, at the Hotel Fontana, with the non-UN and Dutch personnel. That was in the morning of July 12th, 1995. Again, Mr. Beara was not invited, did not participate, and there is no evidence to suggest or infer that he was informed of the contents of that meeting. Mr. Beara's lack of attendance and lack of participation, in our view, confirms his lack of knowledge in the purported crimes that occurred in Srebrenica in 1995. His lack of participation, his lack of attendance, confirms not only his lack of knowledge about the crimes but his lack of knowledge of any purported plan orchestrated by others if such a plan even existed. The Prosecutor, in its briefs and in its indictment, suggest that the plan is something that was a moving target. They suggest that it started as early as 1992, and then he goes on and develops it. The manifestation of this purported plan, which I submit to you there was none. Not my burden of proof, but I submit to you that there was no plan, as the Prosecutor says, to commit genocide, by any of the VRS members and most definitely there was no plan that was ever shared, communicated to, or informed to, to Mr. Beara. The Prosecution, I think, says that Mr. Beara was an empty vessel, an empty vessel isolated on an abandoned ship in the middle of sea. He's telling us two years ago, after eight years of research, eight years of witnesses, eight years of working, and I believe as Mr. Ruez will share with us next week or when he testifies, that there are two people in Mr. Ruez's view who know the Srebrenica case better than anyone. Obviously, the self-serving Mr. Ruez says it is himself, and also his superior, Mr. McCloskey. After eight years at that time, after an additional two years of working this case, Mr. McCloskey again calls him an empty vessel. An empty vessel because he was merely a staff officer, did not participate in any meetings. We agree. The only thing, quite candidly, at this point that we disagree with is that they come up with this vague General Mladic gave some orders. There is no evidence to that. Mr. Beara was never and had never had authority vested in him, expressed or implied, by any commander, had never had any responsibility for the handling of the Bosnian Muslim prisoners taken or captured after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. Mr. Beara had no power or authority to organise, to facilitate, to coordinate or to transport any of the Bosnian Muslims after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. Mr. Beara also had no power or authority to supervise or oversee any of the Bosnian Muslim prisoners captured or taken after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. It's significant when the Prosecutor tells us that he's an empty vessel. It's significant when the Prosecutor tells us that Mr. Beara cannot hold a candle to Mr. Blagojevic. It's significant when we look at the evidence and view each document, how does it fit against or in favour of Mr. Beara? I suggest that the documents where he's not mentioned, where he doesn't appear, plainly and simply put, exonerate Mr. Beara because he was not participating, he was not present, and there is no evidence, as the Prosecutor said a day or so ago, linking him together. They call their chapter 3 The Evidence to Link. He does claim to have some -- rather, or a few intercepts. We've touched on a couple. I invite the Court, obviously respectfully - I know you will - look at those intercepts carefully. He talked about an intercept where Beara's name was mentioned with respect to Mr. Popovic. Mr. Popovic in his discussion, as you will recall, is telling, supposedly Mr. Krstic, they won't let us in, they won't give us access. There is not only more than one reasonable explanation or view on those purported facts, but there are multiple, and this jurisprudence suggests that if the inference can be reasonable in favour of the accused, then that's the reasonable interpretation that we are required and mandated to take. I suggest to you that there is a specific reasonable explanation for the intercepts. I must again stress the intercepts for two reasons. We hope to call an expert relating to the intercepts, to explain specifically the mechanism that goes behind the scenes of taking down such information. We believe this Court will find that the intercepts should not be allowed, that this Court will find that the intercepts are not worthy of the credibility necessary for a criminal trial proceeding, and will reject most if not all of the intercepted conversations. Respectfully, I know I'm speculating, but I believe our expert will confirm the flaws in the intercept analysis, and that's what I expect our evidence to show. Facts, just facts. I have to keep reminding myself that because Madam Prosecutor said it and then sometimes we as lawyers do turn a corner or go on another theory. The fact of the matter is that there are going to be multiple witnesses that testify, as Your Honours know. I've tried to categorise these witnesses into certain groups and subgroups. One category of witnesses that I found easier to follow, and I'll share it with the Court, if I may, and that is the Court -- the group called insiders. It's a fact that there are witnesses, and I think the Prosecutor used the word, called insiders. My view is that there are two subgroups to these witnesses called insiders. The first subgroup is witnesses who believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. You switched off your mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I make one little move and it all falls apart. The first subgroup of these witnesses called insiders are those witnesses who believe the ends justify the means. In essence, they have a result and their entire task is to work towards ultimately obtaining, creating, manufacturing evidence to get that result. The ends do not justify the means, although there are witnesses that you'll find believe that that is actually accurate. Who are those witnesses, by way of brief example? There are many, but because of the limited nature of the time, I'll highlight some. I believe one of them is Mr. Ruez. Mr. Ruez says that he was one of the first investigators to go to Srebrenica, and he's worked on it for eight years. Mr. Ruez never attempted to get what we believe are critical information. Critical information from the security branch, critical information such as Mr. Beara's daily required notes to examine fully what his participation, if any, was, but merely concluded, as the Madam Prosecutor did in her opening. Mr. Ruez, you'll find, is not an expert. His investigation is nothing more, most respectfully, than a one-sided view of the Prosecutor's case, having been the senior investigator for the Prosecutor. His view is totally for collective guilt. And we hope that that will be borne out. Another witness who comes to mind, which is in this category of the ends justify the means, by way of example, is the insider known, or previously known, as the OTP military analyst, Richard Butler. The evidence will show, I believe, that Mr. Butler left the United Nations and this Tribunal and now works for a government which abuses POWs and ignores the international laws governing human rights. In our view, it says a lot about someone and someone's character and integrity when they claim one day to fight for human rights and to protect human rights and then the next day they work for a government who abuses such rights. Our military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ostojic. Please, if you want to confront Mr. Butler with this, you do it when he is present, but please don't do it in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, with the most respect, Your Honour - with the most respect - I agree with you, but I wish there was a court, when Mr. McCloskey called my client a derogatory word two years ago, that someone would also suggest to him not to make a comment like the word "sicko" unless he can confront us with that in a courthouse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are dealing with Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour. Our military expert will expose Mr. Butler's flaws as did the Appellate Court in the Krstic trial. Those are facts, where he works, just facts. The second group or subgroup of insiders are witnesses who utilize information as a commodity. Merchandise. Which they sell or share for a reduction in their prison sentence that they may receive as a result of their own culpability. These witnesses -- am I permitted to name them, Your Honour? Although I won't attack them, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know who they are. Provided we are not contravening any protective measure that has already been put in place by another Trial Chamber, you may proceed, but I don't know who you're going to refer to and I consequently am not in a position to say whether they are protected witnesses in other proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I believe that they are witnesses who are well known and testified openly. These witnesses who are those that in fact utilise information and facts as a commodity because of (redacted) (redacted) Momir Nikolic, in our view, among others. These witnesses are ruthless, and for them, in our view, truth is a meaningless concept. For Mr. Beara and our Defence team, we suggest that truth has no marketplace and that you cannot share or you cannot change, alter, manufacture the truth. The truth yesterday should likewise be the same as today. Our integrity, our character is on the line as well. The Prosecutor yesterday or the day before - I think it was Monday - said he has a witness that is a bald faced liar, but there is some of his testimony that we believe we can use and is credible. I don't understand that concept. I honestly don't. Some of these witnesses that you will hear, if they are liars or bald faced liars, should be rejected in whole. We can't pick and choose, as the Prosecutor, I believe, will do, certain aspects in order to fulfil our burden of proof. If that witness is honestly a bald faced liar as identified by the Prosecutor, charge him with perjury. If he's a bald faced liar, don't ruin your own credibility and call such a witness. These witnesses who I call are salesmen of this commodity and information and merchandise not only lie, they commit perjury, they manipulate evidence, they solicit others to corroborate their own lies with more lies. You'll see from these specific witnesses, and some whom I've mentioned, that they not only will solicit others to corroborate their lies, but they will also obtain from documents information in order to corroborate their lies with more lies. I suggest respectfully that their testimony needs to be fully ventilated. Full ventilation is not possible unless all the notes, all the tapes, all the transcripts, both in prison and with the Office of the Prosecutor in their office when they discussed it, be something that is tendered to the Defence and to Your Honours so that we could see the full picture. Every letter that any of these witnesses received from the Prosecutor should be given to us to see if in those letters they asked about and invited them to testify or hinted to them to testify against any accused. Obviously with the underlying, we believe, suggestion that if you help here, we will help you there. One witness comes to mind drastically: Mr. Deronjic. Mr. Deronjic admitted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for that interruption, Mr. Ostojic, but we needed to discuss something. Please go ahead. You were addressing Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, in our view, Your Honour, you'll see - I think it's in one of the exhibits - his plea agreement. He pled guilty, I believe, to crimes involving Srebrenica but not in 1995. He pled guilty to crimes involving Srebrenica three years earlier, I believe, in 1992. We talk about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was on that case, yes. The agreed facts contained in the plea agreement do not refer to 1995, no. They refer to May, 1992; 8th, 9th, 10th and then 12th of May and the events that preceded the takeover of Srebrenica in April and after but not beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I -- respectfully, I think I agree. I know I agree because that's what I said. They don't apply to 1995, his guilty plea, and here is what troubles us and troubles witnesses who we consider witnesses who give information or use information as a commodity: That witness in particular, if there was anyone vested with authority, vested with power, vested with the ability to control or alter the situation in Srebrenica in 1995, our view is the evidence will show that it was Mr. Deronjic. He got a written, expressed, explicit order and direction from Mr. Karadzic telling him he's in charge of the civilian and the military and in charge to protect the civilians of Srebrenica. The Prosecutor has made a decision not to charge someone in Srebrenica. Or they haven't thus far; they are calling him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a misstatement of the facts. Mr. Deronjic is not put in charge of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, Your Honour -- if I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead but I am familiar with the facts of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought the guidelines were that we don't object, as I didn't to Mr. McCloskey's opening. I object to a lot and almost everything he said in his opening. It's my integrity on the line. I will bring forth the document to the Court. I want to be held accountable to that, as I want them to be as well. There is evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. We'll deal with Deronjic when the time comes, but please do remember that he pleaded guilty to the attack on Glogova and only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I do remember that, but I think if the Court will look at his participation relative to Mr. Beara's participation in 1995, or lack of participation, his attendance at meetings in 1995, and Mr. Beara's lack of attendance in 1995, I think the picture becomes more clear. There is another category of witnesses that I believe we'll see during the trial of this case, and they are what I call finger pointers. It's kind of an awkward word, but finger pointers are in essence people or witnesses who point the finger of guilt. And they will come up to this stand and I think, from reading some of their statements and the transcripts in other cases, what they in essence do is they shift the responsibility that was placed on them, they shift the ultimate culpability that they are exposed to and ultimately their criminal responsibility that attaches with both their position, both their involvement, their attendance, participation and presence during the crimes in Srebrenica in 1995. These finger pointers are probably the same people as those who sell information and sell what they call facts as a commodity. It is similar to when we discussed the lack of participation and lack of attendance at the Hotel Fontana meeting. Carefully, if you listen to that evidence, you'll find that witnesses have a varying view of how things occurred when they occurred, especially Mr. Nikolic who, as early as July 12th, purportedly heard or saw Mr. Karadzic make his gesture -- I mean General Mladic, excuse me, make a gesture that all the Muslims should be killed, and you compare that to another witness who points the finger at an accused such as Mr. Beara and he says he came secretly, inebriated or intoxicated late at night, and he shared with me that he got some purported orders from above. Those witnesses, these finger pointers - and we will try to examine this with the Court's permission - will examine first their ultimate involvement, first their ultimate responsibility, and then see how credible they are when they try to attack or attach or include others in the Prosecutor's web that they seem to be weaving of collective guilt. The finger pointers are quick to implicate and solely for the purpose of concealing and disguising their own criminal responsibility. The fact of the matter is that Mr. Beara did not become vested with any power or authority from any commander at any time and was detached from the battlefield activities, if I can use that military phrase, that regrettably occurred in Srebrenica in 1995. The evidence will show through both our witnesses and the Prosecutor's witnesses, that Mr. Beara at all times was not involved and had no knowledge of the purported plan, the implementation of the plan, or the crimes that occurred. He was not promoted, he was not in the inner circle, he was not in attendance at any relevant meetings; he had no command, no control, and no authority. There is no explicit or expressed order, direction, or communication vesting Mr. Beara with any such authority. The evidence will show that the fact of the matter is that Mr. Beara was helpless. The evidence will show that he was as helpless as the UN Dutch personnel who were present, who were on the scene, who saw what happened, who viewed what happened from time to time but could not and did not prevent, stop or deter the horrific crimes that were occurring. In several articles I've heard this term "empty vessel," and they refer to people just like the UN Dutch Battalion or the UN Dutch personnel who were there but unable, with an inability to do anything to prevent such a crime. We believe that Mr. Beara was just as helpless. Given his upbringing, his past education, his work experience, his altercations with the Serbs and the Serbian political aspect in 1992, 1993, and also you'll hear what happened in August of 1995, August 16 specifically - and we'll get to that evidence, but in the view of time I'm summarising it for you - that Mr. Beara, given all those things, given the lack of any documentation, intercepts or witnesses - credible witnesses, honest witnesses, witnesses who don't have something to sell, who don't have anything to gain - that it is not a wonder why Mr. Beara was helpless, powerless, and without authority. Mr. Beara, in our view, and the evidence will prove, is not guilty. I tried to highlight -- and we are going to call a military expert, as I said. I want to expose what it means not to be able to hold a candle to Mr. Blagojevic. I know my time is running short. I want to be kept to our agreement, and I appreciate you for listening. I want to expose and also further explain or try to discuss with the Court throughout this trial what this "empty vessel" means. Those are their words, not ours. I want to expose the fact that there are no documentation, intercepts, or witnesses other than those that are incredible, meaning a lack of credibility in my view, and most respectfully, when they implicate or finger point or actually claim that the ends justify the means. We will try to show this Court in about a year or so, I'm not sure what the schedule is, specifically that evidence with respect to Mr. Beara. I appreciate your patience with me. I appreciate and have the confidence, the utmost confidence, respectfully, that this Court will wait before they make a decision and not listen to one-sided evidence before they ultimately review that. I know you know your responsibilities. I'm saying it perhaps for my benefit more than others: Hold us to what we say in this courtroom. Hold the Prosecutor that their view is that specific intent flows with your job. It doesn't exist. Hold them when he says that Mr. Beara can't hold a candle to Mr. Blagojevic. Hold us to the promises that I've made to you with respect to some of our witnesses and some of the evidence that I hope we will share with you in the next coming months. On behalf of Mr. Beara and our Defence team, we thank you for listening and we look forward to presenting our case to you in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question before you sit down, Mr. Ostojic. You -- a very few minute ago, or two, you made reference to some event going back to August 16, 1995. What event are you referring to? Particularly because I don't think you gave us an indication of what that is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's a great question. I wanted to pique everyone's curiosity, like the September 1992 and 1993 event. In 1995, specifically August 16th, 1995, there is some evidence to suggest - a document in particular - that Mr. Beara sent to the supreme military court, asking that they appoint specific investigators and deputy prosecutors to investigate certain war crimes or prisoners that were held who were ultimately going to be transferred to Foca. I was going to share with you specifically the details of those three meetings and how in one meeting the UN, I think, witnesses will also say that General Mladic ordered - ordered - that the prisoners that were captured, the military prisoners, those who participated with the ABiH, that they be interrogated for war crimes. That act, actually, and part of our Defence is, shows that in fact there was activity, that people were put down on a list, people were interrogated, people were investigated. We think that all comes home for the Defence. Now the Prosecution promised you something also. They said there is no evidence that anyone was interrogated. We are going to call a Dutch witness, we believe, who will tell the Court contrary. He saw it. He observed it. He even participated in it during the critical time period. I didn't think it was necessary to share every aspect, but quite frankly, I can, I think, and we will. But this is a critical thing, so what we are trying to show before, during, and after, I think it's an enormously relevant document, a document that should not be ignored by the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. I now give the floor to the Defence team for Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. We will have a break at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could suggest that we have a break right now. I need just to do a little technical set-up and change seats because I have presentations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll have a 20-minute break starting from now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. You reckon you'll be speaking for how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I anticipate that I will need the two hours, even though I will try to cut down on some parts of my presentation which have been covered by my colleague representing the Accused Beara. I would maybe propose that we start for one hour, take a short break, and then continue for a second hour and I will finish for sure within the two-hour limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And all know that it's not a question of restricting the time limit. We will need about ten minutes at the end of this sitting to address -- to discuss something with you which is pretty much urgent that relates to the planning, the scheduling of witnesses. Thanks. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I begin this opening statement, I would like to make two apologies before this Trial Chamber. The first one to my colleagues on the Prosecution for what I said on Monday when I was introducing a motion for reconsideration when I was convinced that we had not received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go straight to your opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The second thing, Mr. President, is simply to say that I have been informed by the people who work behind the windows that I spoke very fast on Monday. I will try to speak slower but I have a little more than five minutes this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the interpreters should be thankful that you're speaking English and not French because my experience with you is that when you speak French, you speak it even faster. Anyway, yes, thank you, Mr. Bourgon, and please do try to keep that -- the -- in the back of your mind all the time because the interpreters' job is extremely, extremely difficult. So if we try to cooperate, cooperate with them as much as we can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Plein de la cour, Mr. President, Honourable Judges, it is both an honour and a privilege for me to stand up before you this morning in this courtroom. As you know, I've been associated with this Tribunal for many, many years - not as many as my colleague from the Prosecution, but quite close - and I believe in the work of this Tribunal. Of course there have been and there continues to be frustrations in working before this Tribunal. And I'm sure you will agree with me, Mr. President, that it is not easy to be a Defence counsel before the ICTY. I think this is due mostly because of the nature and the objective gravity of the charges and the accusations which are adjudicated before the ICTY. What I can say, however, without any hesitation is that I am proud to be here this morning. And the main reason why I am so proud is because I believe in the work I do. I believe in the necessity of this work, and I believe that there is an absolute requirement for Defence counsel. Contrary to popular belief, it is not because you are accused before the ICTY that you are guilty. It must be, and it is, possible for an accused to be acquitted of charges if these charges are not proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Today it is my duty to introduce the case for the Defence of 2nd Lieutenant Drago Nikolic, and I'm accompanied for this purpose this morning by Ms. Jelena Nikolic and by Bojan Stefanovic. You heard me right, Mr. President, when I said 2nd Lieutenant Drago Nikolic. I did not say general. I did not say colonel. And I did not say lieutenant colonel, major, or captain. In fact, I did not even say lieutenant. I said 2nd Lieutenant Drago Nikolic, a man accused of conspiracy to commit genocide. Now, this is significant. As you may also know, I spent many years in the military - more than 20, as a matter of fact - and I have no doubt in telling you this morning that there is very little a second lieutenant can do in any army of the world in terms of deciding the course of action of this army. My aim in presenting this opening statement this morning, of course, is to provide you with an overview of what can be expected to be presented and what we will hear during this trial in relation to 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic. To begin, there are two preliminary issues I would like to raise, the first one being the Prosecutor's address before my colleague took the floor from the Prosecution. Now, Mrs. Del Ponte, what did she say? Well, she said something that cannot be denied as we begin this trial, and that is that many persons were killed in the Srebrenica area in July, 1995, and that what happened in that region can be described as anything -- cannot be described as anything less than a tragedy. Now, we don't agree that this is a genocide, and we don't agree with the numbers of unlawfully killed persons or victims as alleged by the Prosecutor. But a tragedy it was. That is undisputable, and we offer our most sincere condolences and support to the families which were broken as a result. In this, Mr. President, Honourable Judges, we fully agree with Madam Prosecutor Del Ponte. Where we also agree with her is that the crimes associated with Srebrenica must not be imputed on the Bosnian Serbs as a people, nor on the army of Republika Srpska as an organisation, nor on any other entity or group, but solely on individuals. Individual criminal responsibility is the business of this Tribunal and it is also the aim of this Tribunal. And at the end of the day, at the end of this trial, none of the accused who stand here before you should be held accountable unless it is proven beyond a reasonable doubt - and I weigh my words - that they personally and individually committed the crimes they are charged with. Proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Words highly familiar, highly familiar to anyone who has studied law in any way. But also, regrettably, Mr. President, words the meaning of which is often misunderstood, if not forgotten, by many jurists, and that is for various reasons. Now, unfortunately in this case, despite the Prosecutor's statement or reassurance that no organisation is on trial here, this is not what stems from the Prosecution's strategy, nor from the Prosecution's opening statement. I'll get back to this a little later when I address the issue of joint criminal enterprise, which, strangely, yes, but understandably, was not even mentioned once by my colleague from the Prosecution during his opening statement. Allow me, Mr. President, simply to make a quick reference to the opening statement where my colleague from the Prosecution stated, "We don't believe the Serbs' story." That was when he was discussing the alleged involvement of one of the accused in this case and there was a story about somebody grabbing a gun and getting his hands burnt. It's not the witness that the Prosecution doesn't believe. Unfortunately, it is the Serbs' story. That is significant, and this is not right. The second preliminary issue I wish to address at this time is the reason why we decided to address Your Honours this morning at the beginning of the trial and not to wait until the end of the Prosecution's case. Of course this is our choice and we exercise our option to do it today. But why do we decide to do so? We debated the issue. It's a matter of strategy, our many theories, and it is not an easy decision to decide to do this opening statement today. The fact that we are appearing before professional Judges is, of course, a major consideration. I'd like to share with you the two governing factors that made us decide to go before you today with this opening statement. The first one is the unique character of this case. Why is this case so unique? Well, it's unique because it has received world-wide media attention. Maybe using the word "this case" is not the right word to use, but the events in Srebrenica have certainly received world-wide media attention. Two previous trials have been held in which a general, commander of the Drina Corps, General Krstic, was found guilty; and a second trial was held during which the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Colonel Blagojevic, and the chief of the engineers within the Zvornik Brigade, and that is Jokic, were both found guilty. The Prosecutor has labelled this -- the events of Srebrenica as a largest killing operation in Europe. What we want to avoid is simply to consider that because there have been past trials, this trial will be the same and that its result will be the same. I mentioned in the pre-trial brief the SALT principle, or guilt based on Same As Last Trial. Unless guilt has been proven in this case, in this trial, then there is no guilt. This is a different trial. My colleague from the Prosecution also mentioned that no one will be left untouched by the proceedings here, and I agree with him. We will see horrible pictures and we will hear some pretty ugly stories. But it is our duty, everyone here in this courtroom, to get over these pictures and to assess what we are here to assess, and that is the alleged responsibility of the people who stand accused before you. Now, there are a number of co-accused in this case and that also makes this case quite unique. Beyond any doubt the Prosecution would like to sit there and to watch the co-accused in this case take on each other and fight each other and he can just sit and wait for a guilty verdict. It is probably the strongest aspect of his case, at least in his view, but it would not be right for the Prosecution to try and prove its case in this manner. The onus and the burden is on the Prosecution to prove this case. Now, these are the things that make this case unique and this is the first governing factor why we decided to go today. The second one is that we want or we decided to alert the Trial Chamber from the beginning of the case on the following: First, the other side of the story. This will be a long trial. Much of the evidence for the Defence will come in during the Prosecution phase. It will come in through cross-examinations and it will come in by the Prosecution's own witnesses. There are weaknesses in the Prosecution's case and there are potential traps to be avoided by all. That is why we decided that it was necessary for us to alert you of these issues before the beginning of the trial. Now, I was listening, of course, as you were to my colleagues from the Prosecution on Monday and Tuesday. And it is clear when you listen to the Prosecution that it has lost its objectivity. Every bit of evidence, every document, is being seen, analysed and interpreted against the accused without any consideration for the opposite view. But this is not surprising. It's the Prosecution's duty, as Madam Del Ponte said, on behalf of the international community, to prosecute persons alleged to be the most responsible. Now, even though we will again and again hear from the Prosecution that they are here to establish the truth, we should not be misled. This is not so. The Prosecution is here to prosecute and it will do everything in its power to ensure that the persons who stand before you today are found guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object -- this is a direct attack on the ethics of the Prosecution. I object at this time because if this kind of personal attacks are allowed to continue, this trial will become a travesty and a circus. And if it's allowed now, it will continue and continue and continue, and it's just completely unsubstantiated and uncalled for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that the word you're taking objection at is the misled, that you're being -- the Prosecution is being attributed misleading --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He said we are not looking for the truth, we are looking to mislead you and prosecute people with no regard for the truth. That's what he said. And that is outrageous. If it's allowed to continue, it will corrupt this system and it will become a circus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a consultation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, it's the agreement here, unanimous agreement, that you should approach your criticism of the Prosecution in a completely different manner. We wouldn't like you to repeat what you have said, basically that the Prosecution is deliberately seeking to mislead the Trial Chamber by -- and also not being interested in seeking the truth. I think that's an attack on the integrity of the Prosecution which should be avoided. And I'm sure that you are capable of avoiding and addressing the -- avoiding these -- addressing these issues the same way you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like simply to say that I do not believe that I've said anything outrageous. I did not say that the Prosecution is trying to mislead. I said that we should not be misled in what the role and the duty of the Prosecution was, and I also said that the Prosecution would do everything in its power. I did not say that the Prosecution was doing something illegal. I did not say that the Prosecution was not having integrity. And I don't really appreciate, as was said by my colleague, being interrupted by Mr. McCloskey during my opening statement when I did not say anything wrong. However, Mr. President, if you believe that I did go beyond what is proper for this opening statement, I gladly accept your ruling and will refrain from any further comments in this way in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are sure you will, Mr. Bourgon. Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I continue my opening statement simply by saying that facing the Prosecution nonetheless, you have the Defence. And the aim of the Defence, of course, is to try and balance things out. But more importantly, Mr. President, there is you, the Trial Chamber, whose duty it is to assess and weigh the evidence with a view to deciding if the accused before you today, if 2nd Lieutenant Drago Nikolic bears any criminal responsibility for what happened in Srebrenica area in 1995. And that's why we decided to do our opening statement, to ensure that every bit, every iota of evidence as it is admitted in this trial, whether in the form of documents, witness testimony or other, is assessed in full knowledge that there are two opposing theories in this case. Now, I refer you to this picture on your screen. This, Mr. President, is the boring figure. It's a drawing dating back to 1915. You may have recognised the young lady on this drawing. Unless, of course, you recognise the old lady with her chin down in her collar. This picture, which really contains two images, was made to show that the human brain can only recognise one of the two images at a time. But just as for the Prosecution's theory, there is another story behind what the Prosecution would like you to see exclusively. Whenever the Prosecution will show you the young lady, we respectfully submit that we must also be looking for the old. And when the Prosecution will be attempting to show you the old lady, we respectfully submit that we must also look for the young. This is a critical aspect of this case. With this in mind, I now turn to the outline of my opening statement which is displayed on the screen before you, divided into two parts. In the first part I would like to address some of the highlights in the Prosecution opening statements, to discuss the accused, Drago Nikolic, who he is, and to look at the case against Drago Nikolic so that we are clear about what the issues are in this case. In the second part, after a brief break, if you allow for such a break, then we will look at the applicable law, we will look at the Prosecution's theory and the case for the Defence, and finally I will conclude by looking at the evidence which you will hear in this case from both parties. Moving straight on to the first topic, highlights of the Prosecution's opening statement. It's not my intention to spend too much time on the Prosecution's opening statement, but there are some issues which must be mentioned before we hear the first witness. Firstly, although my colleague spoke for some hours, I would not be surprised in this case if the Trial Chamber was somewhat worried as the Prosecution's statement appears, with all due respect and at least in our view, rather thin. Even though I suspect that my colleague may have done this on purpose, this is nonetheless revealing at this stage. The Prosecution does have a theory, but very little relevant evidence was referred to in support of this story. This is very much like its pre-trial brief; the telling of a tragedy, supported by exhibits which were presented in other cases but without reference to exhibits in this case. Not surprisingly, the interpretation offered at this stage is very much one-sided, and in this I join my colleague representing the accused Beara that there are indeed other reasonable and more plausible interpretations to these documents as the evidence will show. Strikingly, other than to say that one of its witnesses is a bald faced liar and warning the Trial Chamber that witnesses will go back and forth, not telling the truth, very little reference has been made to witness evidence. More importantly, the theme of the Prosecution's case was described on the basis of a document as being the success of the VRS in Srebrenica, Zepa, and other fronts. While this has little to do with 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic as an individual, it certainly has something to do with him as a member of the VRS. Simply put, Mr. President, the evidence will show that the success of the VRS from a military standpoint is not a joint criminal enterprise. Amazingly, and as mentioned earlier, these words, "joint criminal enterprise," the focus and the skeleton of the Prosecution's theory, without which this trial would be entirely different, have been omitted altogether from the opening statement. As we will see, this is significant. As for other highlights which we believe the Trial Chamber must be made aware of at this stage, these include the following: First, the importance of the operational logs has been underscored at length, yet the Prosecution has only translated a very limited number of pages of these logs. We wish to take this opportunity to inform the Trial Chamber that we will object to any request to have selected entries of these logs entered in evidence out of context. The importance of the intercept material has also been highlighted by the Prosecution in its opening statement. We also take this opportunity that even though these are, at least to this day -- or there are, sorry, at least to this day and to your knowledge, no intercept material involving 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic, this material will be contested and that this will require that intercepts not be considered a la piece but in the proper context. In its opening the Prosecution has referred to the differences between the functions of commander, deputy commander, assistant commander, staff officer. The Prosecution has also made reference to the duties and responsibility of the security branch as well as to the military functions of intelligence and counter-intelligence. We take this opportunity to inform the Trial Chamber that the evidence in this case will portray a situation which is different from that described by the Prosecution. And we believe that this is important for the Trial Chamber to know this before the testimony of any witness employed in such functions testify. Lastly, under this topic, in its opening statement, the Prosecution has made reference to documents not available because they have been destroyed. This is significant. In fact, we agree that some documents are missing because they have been destroyed. Furthermore, as regards 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic, we will go as far as to say that the missing documents in this case will be more important than some of the exhibits on the record, especially when the time comes to assess and draw inferences regarding the conduct of 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic. Simply put, the evidence presented in this case will show that many of the documents from the Zvornik Brigade available have been carefully selected by one of the Prosecution witnesses, and that other documents which are important for the understanding of this case have been disposed of we don't know how. I now move on to my second topic of the first part, which is the identity and the character of the accused, 2nd Lieutenant Drago Nikolic. Again in this regard I join my colleague representing the accused Beara in stressing the fact and the importance of knowing the background of the accused when considering the evidence related to his conduct. So who is Drago Nikolic? To provide but a summary at this stage, it is our submission that the evidence will show the following regarding

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Born in 1957 in the village of Brana Bacici - sorry for the pronunciation - in the municipality of Bratunac. That means that he was 37 years old at the time in July, 1995. He has two brothers -- well, actually he has three, because one died very young. At the age of 14, Drago Nikolic, unlike his brothers, was sent to secondary military school. That is from 1972 to 1976. He did not go to college. Immediately following high school, he began serving in the infantry. That is in 1976. Having served eight years in the infantry, he requested to attend a basic policing course at the military security training centre in Pancevo. That's a short course of three and a half months. And that is why in 1985 he was appointed to the position of assistant in the military police with the rank of senior sergeant. As senior sergeant, this is a non-officer rank. Three years later, because he was a good senior sergeant, he became a 1st class sergeant. And in 1991, he served as a member of the military security branch at the Sarajevo garrison. Drago Nikolic is married and the father of two daughters. In 1990, shortly before the war, he lost his son, who died at the age of eight, which was a very difficult event. Due to the war, Drago Nikolic was sent to Zvornik where he became assistant commander for security, a post normally occupied by an officer at the rank of major. Way above his level of responsibility at the time. Because this was an officer's position, he was given the rank of 2nd lieutenant, which he retained throughout the war, and when he retired in 1998 he still had not been promoted to a higher rank. Today, Drago Nikolic has three granddaughters. We respectfully suggest to you, Mr. President, Honourable Judges, that this information will be highly relevant as you set out to assess whether he should bear any responsibility for the events that unfolded during the three days for which he has been charged by the Prosecutor. Of course, Mr. President, it's also important to look at the duties and responsibilities assumed by Drago Nikolic during this period. The evidence in this case will show the difference between an assistant commander and the chief of a department such as, for example, the chief of communications. The evidence will also show the difference between the functions of intelligence and counter-intelligence. To provide an idea, the intelligence officer in any military unit is there to gather information and to assess the actions of the enemy with a view to interpreting this information and providing the commander with an assessment of the strength, the weaknesses, and the likely actions of the enemy. Intelligence is a vital function in any army, as well as a highly specialised trade. As for the counter-intelligence function, as indicated by its name, this refers to the measures taken to frustrate the gathering of intelligence by the enemy. It implies the search for sources used by the enemy to gather information and to take measures to try and put an end to such information gathering. We respectfully suggest, Mr. President, that the difference between intelligence and counter-intelligence is highly relevant here. Why is this so? Well, simply because the two functions can, in some cases, be performed by the same persons, depending on the type and size of the unit or formation. This was the case, for example, as the evidence will show, for Momir Nikolic. Within the Bratunac Brigade, Momir Nikolic was a security officer and he took care of intelligence and he took care of counter-intelligence. This was not the case for Drago Nikolic. As assistant commander for security, he performed the counter-intelligence function but not the intelligence function. This is significant because, in this capacity, Drago Nikolic had limited information at his disposal with regard to what was going on elsewhere within the Drina Corps. This is also significant because, as mentioned by the Prosecution in its opening, counter-intelligence officers do not have subordinates or personnel. Expert evidence in this trial will show and explain in detail the responsibility of security officers. Expert evidence -- expert witness evidence will confirm that, contrary to the Prosecution's assertions, security officers do not command, direct, or manage military police resources within the unit or formation. Their role is to advise the commander on the employment of the military police resources, but the commander, or in his absence the deputy commander, as was often the case in Zvornik Brigade, retains full authority to employ the military police resources as he sees fit. In this regard, orders can be issued directly to the commander of the military police company without informing the assistant commander for security. Simply put, Drago Nikolic had no authority over the military police company and could not issue orders to a man called Jasikovac, the commander of the military police company. This, we take the view, is highly relevant here and will be shown by the evidence. In its opening statement, or maybe it is in the pre-trial brief, the Prosecution stated that Drago Nikolic was responsible for all prisoners within the zone of responsibility of Zvornik Brigade. At this time, suffice it to say that we will challenge this assertion and expert witness evidence will demonstrate that the concept of zone of responsibility is not a term which finds application in this regard. Expert witness testimony will also establish clearly for which prisoners or persons detained the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade could be responsible. I now move on to part 3 -- or, sorry, topic 3 of part 1, which is the Prosecution's case against Drago Nikolic. Now, no matter how we look at the latest amended indictment, it appears evident that the Prosecution's case against Drago Nikolic can be found in paragraphs 42 and 80 of the indictment. To save some time I will not quote these paragraphs but I will simply indicate to you that they are highly similar. Paragraph 42 would be the actions of Drago Nikolic with respect to the first joint criminal enterprise, while paragraph 80 would be the actions of Drago Nikolic much the same for the second joint criminal enterprise. It is on this basis - two paragraphs - that the Prosecution is asking you, or will be asking you, after the presentation of its case, to convict Drago Nikolic for all charges in the indictment because he was allegedly a member of a joint criminal enterprise to transfer the population of both Srebrenica and Zepa and a second joint criminal enterprise to kill a number of men and boys from Srebrenica. As we will explain a little later, and as the evidence will demonstrate in this case, even if the evidence established paragraphs 42 and 80 beyond a reasonable doubt, which we respectfully submit will not be the case, Drago Nikolic could not be found to be a member of the two alleged joint criminal enterprises. The Prosecution's shotgun approach must also be addressed in this regard. As mentioned in our pre-trial brief, it is simply not right for the Prosecution to allege all possible forms of liability pursuant to the statute without stating clearly what its case is. As we can see from a number of indictments before this Tribunal, Drago Nikolic's case is not an isolated event in this regard. This is like if the Prosecution took a number of pieces of one euro, threw everything in the air, and then tried to catch them. Hoping, of course, that something will fall in the end. We respectfully ask you, Mr. President, Honourable Judges, to be critical in your analysis of the evidence as it will be produced by both parties, with a view to seeing through the overcharging policy of the Prosecutor in respect of Drago Nikolic. I've been speaking for about 45 minutes and I'm about to go into part 2. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you, Mr. Bourgon, but if you prefer a break now, we'll grant you a break now. If you can move to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I can begin on the second part, and once we hit one hour, then I suggest we stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You started your intervention at 10.35, so regulate accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. So moving on to part 2, the first topic is the applicable law in this case.
