The Prosecution has not addressed the applicable law in its opening statement but it has done so in its pre-trial brief. Without spending too much time on this topic, there are indeed legal issues which we believe must be brought to the attention of the Trial Chamber at this stage. The Trial Chamber will not be surprised that the first of these issues is the joint criminal enterprise form of liability as alleged and pleaded by the Prosecution. In its opening statement, Prosecution said: "We are all familiar with the crime of drugs and the crime of bank robbery." Even though this was not mentioned, it is our understanding that the joint criminal enterprise is what my colleague had in mind when saying this. And I must agree with him, which, as the Trial Chamber may have appreciated, is not something which happens to me too often, that drugs and bank robbery are indeed crimes well suited to the application of the joint criminal enterprise doctrine. This is the classical example: Three persons set out to rob a bank. They each have a loaded gun. They each perform a different task or function which is part of the bank robbery. One of the three encounters a security guard, even if that was unexpected, and he shoots him. As a result, the three are convicted of bank robbery pursuant to JCE category 1, and the three are also convicted of murder under joint criminal enterprise category 3, because even though murder was not part of the original plan, it was a natural and foreseeable consequence of the implementation of the plan. Now, of course, there can be many variables added to this example, such as, upon setting out to implement the joint criminal enterprise of robbing a bank, the three had an unloaded gun, and this was confirmed by the three of them before they set out, and it's only after they left each other that one of the three, without telling the others, loaded his gun. In this example, it could be argued that the murder was not a natural and foreseeable consequence of the joint criminal enterprise. I take the time to go -- to mention this, Mr. President, because the difficulty is trying to apply the same doctrine to a much more complex situation and to make everyone or all members of the VRS guilty, whoever they are and whatever they do, if they happen to be present in the Srebrenica area or in the Zvornik area in July, 1995. When the joint criminal enterprise or common purpose doctrine was first used before the International Tribunal, that was in the Tadic case, even though this was more complex than a bank robbery, it could be understood why Tadic was found guilty of murder committed during an operation conducted in a village despite the fact that there was no evidence as to who had committed these murders. The joint criminal enterprise doctrine was born. The problem is that ever since the Prosecution has been pushing the envelope again and again to expand the joint criminal enterprise liability concept to ensure that all members of any group are found guilty. In this case, it appears on the Prosecution's pleading that if you are a member of the Main Staff, you are automatically guilty; or with respect to Drago Nikolic, if you are a member of the security branch or of the Zvornik Brigade, you are also guilty. In fact, Mr. President, it appears as though we are getting into strict liability, and this simply cannot be. Not surprisingly, in Prosecution circles, the joint criminal enterprise liability concept is referred to as the just-convict-everyone liability concept. This is why as we begin this trial, it is important to establish clearly what elements have to be established beyond a reasonable doubt for Drago Nikolic to be found guilty pursuant to a joint criminal enterprise mode of liability. I suggest, Mr. President, that we stop here and then I will continue to finish in less than one hour in the second part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Bourgon. We'll have a 20-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Honourable Judges. I will continue where I left off and that was in the overview of the joint criminal enterprise form of liability. Now, in its decision on the form of the indictment issued on, I think it was 12 or 13 July, the Trial Chamber partly addressed this issue and confirmed that pursuant to this mode of liability, it is not compulsory for the perpetrator to have been involved in the actus reus of the crime. We agree. However, there are other elements which must be established not the least being the clear identification of the joint criminal enterprise, or common purpose, the participation of the accused in this common purpose, and more importantly, the mens rea, and that it must be shown that the accused himself intended the crime at issue to be committed. With this in mind, we respectfully suggest that the evidence will demonstrate that the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer all Muslims from Srebrenica and Zepa, as alleged and pleaded by the Prosecution, does not fulfil these requirements. Moreover, in the event that a similar joint criminal enterprise was established, or was focused on a right common purpose, the evidence will show that Drago Nikolic was never a party to this joint criminal enterprise and certainly never intended to further the alleged common purpose of forcibly transferring the Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa. The Trial Chamber has ruled -- sorry. Furthermore, Mr. President, we need to address the category 3 of joint criminal enterprise, and we respectfully submit that the evidence offered in this trial by the Prosecution and the Defence alike will demonstrate that the opportunistic killings as pleaded by the Prosecution were not the natural and foreseeable consequences of carrying out both common purposes as alleged. Now, this is linked, as you probably recall, Mr. President, to a previous decision of the Trial Chamber for which certification was not granted, and the issue at stake was whether a joint criminal enterprise requires the physical perpetrator has an agreement with the accused who is charged as a participant and whether the physical perpetrator has to be a participant in the joint criminal enterprise himself. The Trial Chamber has ruled that the latter is an issue that will have to be addressed at trial. While we are confident that this issue will soon be determined in other proceedings before the International Tribunal, we consider it important to respectfully state, as we begin this trial, that in our view there must be an agreement and that the physical perpetrator must be a participant himself because this is the only way to avoid strict liability. The Defence of 2nd Lieutenant Nikolic does not dispute -- that's moving on to another topic, which is genocide -- the essential elements of genocide as they have been developed by the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal. However, we do dispute the manner in which these elements have to be applied to the facts not only of this case but of every case with a view to determining whether or not a genocide was committed. We do not believe that the Srebrenica events amount to a genocide and we will be calling on expert witness evidence with the aim of providing the Trial Chamber with the necessary frame of analysis to assist it in determining whether a genocide has taken place or not. Of course, we can't speak about genocide without looking at the charge that was laid for conspiracy to commit genocide against 2nd Lieutenant Drago Nikolic. As was mentioned before, this is not an accusation that is a regular before the International Tribunal, and in this sense we are somewhat entering new territory. Conspiracy to commit genocide has been -- is a charge which has been laid and has been addressed before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, so we have some kind of reference, although the situation that took place in Rwanda in 1994 is far different from the Srebrenica events. Regarding Drago Nikolic, we are of the view that whether or not a conspiracy to commit genocide is established by the evidence, the evidence will show that he could not, did not, and certainly did not have the necessary mens rea to have anything to do with such a conspiracy. At this stage there is only one last legal issue I wish to address before moving on to my next topic, and that is the apparent confusion which the Prosecution is making between what is known as jus ad bellum and jus in bello. It can be anticipated that during this trial, again and again, the Prosecution will be driving home the issue of joint criminal enterprise and the allegation that all members of the VRS were part of it. We are of the view, however, Mr. President, that a distinction must be made between the strategic and military objectives of the VRS, which may potentially be seen as violations of the right to use force in Bosnia in 1995, but that such violations of public international law, or jus in bello -- sorry, are not violations of humanitarian law or jus in bello and cannot be the basis of a joint criminal enterprise. To us, this distinction -- will be necessary to maintain this distinction throughout this trial. I now move on to the second topic of my second part, and that is the Prosecution's theory of the case regarding Drago Nikolic. As mentioned, on the basis of the allegations in paragraphs 42 and 80 of the indictment, the Prosecution has charged Drago Nikolic and will ask you, after introducing its evidence, to find him guilty of the following: As a participant in the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the population from Srebrenica and Zepa; secondly, to find him guilty of all the crimes beyond this joint criminal enterprise alleged as being the natural and foreseeable consequences of this common purpose; thirdly, as a participant in the joint criminal enterprise to kill thousands of men and boys from Srebrenica; and finally, of all the crimes beyond this joint criminal enterprise which were the natural or alleged to be the natural and foreseeable consequences of accomplishing this common purpose. With all due respect for my colleagues from the Prosecution, it is our submission today, as the evidence will show, that this is simply a leap too far. More importantly, that such a conclusion does not match, nor fit, the Prosecution's theory of the case even before we set out to hear the first witness. It must be recalled in this regard some of the assertions made by the Prosecution in its opening statement. First, the fact that the strategic objective of the VRS were developed and remained unchanged since 1992. Secondly, that the plan to kill the men from Potocari would have been adopted by Mladic on the night of the 11th July. Thirdly, that the plan to kill all of the other prisoners would have been adopted on 12 July, and that the executions would have begun on 13 July in the morning. Number 5: That the initial decision to perform some of these executions in the Zvornik area would have been made in the afternoon of 13 July. And 6, that the information related to these killings would have reached Zvornik not before the night of 13 July. These are assertions that we will say will not be demonstrated by the evidence. But for the sake of argument, let's say they are. It is our submission today that these assertions, as a minimum, defeat the Prosecution's case that Drago Nikolic was a participant in the first joint criminal enterprise. It is also our submission that whoever committed these killings in the Zvornik area, the evidence will show that this was not a Zvornik Brigade-led operation, even though the evidence will show that some resources from that brigade were indeed used. More importantly, regarding Drago Nikolic personally, the evidence will show that he was not a participant in these events. More specifically, it appears that the Prosecution's case, when we look at what the case is, what we've heard from my colleague on Monday and Tuesday, to find him guilty of all crimes in the indictment, appears to be as follows: A telephone conversation with the deputy commander of Zvornik Brigade, of which there is no intercept evidence; a decision by the deputy commander to relieve him from duty at the forward command post on the night of 13 July so that he could participate. There is only one witness who will say that, and it's the person who says he was relieved from duty. The fact that he was seen in Orahovac by some witnesses, a vehicle log which shows that a vehicle from the security travelled to some of the execution sites. But the Prosecution has said they cannot and will not be able to show that Drago Nikolic was ever in that vehicle. Finally, an entry in the Zvornik Brigade log where the name of Drago Nikolic appears close to that of the accused Beara. Of course, this is not an exhaustive list of the evidence which will be presented in this trial against Drago Nikolic, but very close to it, and it is on this basis that they will ask you to find Drago Nikolic guilty of all crimes in the indictment. There is, as I've mentioned at the beginning, another side to this story and this will be revealed by the evidence which will leave you no choice but to conclude that Drago Nikolic is not the man the Prosecution would like you to believe he is. The case for the Defence will show that there was no telephone conversation between the deputy commander of Zvornik Brigade and Drago Nikolic, and the evidence will show that Drago Nikolic was not relieved from his forward command post duty on the night of 13 July to participate in these events. The evidence will also demonstrate that Drago Nikolic was not informed of the infamous plan, if I may refer to the plan this way, on the night of 13 July by Momir Nikolic from Bratunac Brigade. The case for the Defence will also provide information on the whereabouts of Drago Nikolic during the three days for which he is now charged with genocide. Was he in the Zvornik Brigade area? Yes, he was, and the evidence will show that. Will you hear some witnesses saying that he was in Zvornik Brigade area? Yes, you will hear that. We will have to assess where he was at what time. Having said this, I now turn to the last topic of the second part which is exactly looking at the Prosecution evidence in this case. Looking at documentary evidence, I have already addressed this issue earlier, and I've informed the Trial Chamber that we will be contesting the reliability of the intercept material as well as the danger of drawing inferences from such material. To provide but one example: While the Trial Chamber in the Krstic case, on the basis of one intercept, concluded that Krstic was involved in the killing operation, the Appeals Chamber reversed this finding on the basis that the intercept used could have another meaning and that this was not enough. This applies to the interpretation of many documents, as suggested by the Prosecution. We respectfully ask you, Mr. President, Honourable Judges, to keep in mind the other reasonable and often more plausible interpretations possible. I also take this opportunity to reiterate once again the importance of the missing documents, as well as why these documents are missing, which brings me to the witness issue, the witness who will be called by the Prosecution in this case. Of course, there are many types of witnesses that you will hear. You will hear victims. And it is our undertaking before you today that we will show the greatest of respect for witnesses who are victims of the events in Srebrenica. We will try to show compassion as best as we can and we will try to limit our cross-examination of these witnesses. Nonetheless, the tendency of a victim to inflate numbers, something quite normal, and to say more than what really happened is something we have to be careful with. You will hear expert witnesses from both the Prosecution and the Defence. That's not a problem. Expert witnesses may be required to assist the Trial Chamber in performing its adjudicating function, as long as those expert witnesses stay within the confines of their area of expertise, and the Defence will see to it that witnesses or expert witnesses from the Prosecution remain within the confines of their expertise. We will hear investigators, members and staff members of the Prosecution who will testify. We think that this is somewhat of a contentious issue. Then again, if these witnesses remain within the confines of providing evidence, there will not be a problem. If they try to step outside of the boundaries of evidence, then for sure the Defence will be there to object. There are, of course, more important categories of witnesses. And these are, first of all, the witnesses who in some way were involved and the insiders. Let's look at the witnesses who were involved. Prosecution has said my own witnesses will be -- will come and go. One of them is a bald faced liar. The Prosecution says the bald face liar witness can bring good evidence that we should keep and we should reject what -- the evidence that does not fit the Prosecution's case. Well, we disagree. The Prosecutor will have to live with the evidence as it comes in. Many people in the Zvornik area were close to what happened. You will hear this from witnesses. Some people may actually have seen what happened. Some people, then again, were personally involved. They are not accused but they were personally involved in these events. To provide but one example, some people, some witnesses will come and say, "I buried those people." It's tough for these witnesses to come and say that. But all of these witnesses, Mr. President, Honourable Judges, have something in common: They are scared beyond any imaginable way because, whether or not they were involved, they are scared that they may be the next people accused to appear in Sarajevo. There is a cloud which hangs over the Zvornik area today. Something which makes it that witnesses who were in the Zvornik area in 1995 are people who would like to forget what they saw, if they were eye-witnesses, what they learned from others, if it's just hearsay, or what they did if they were involved. All of these people are likely to have personal reasons for saying what they will say, whether it is exonerating evidence or inculpatory evidence. It will be a most difficult task for the Trial Chamber to try to make the choice or to weigh the evidence that will be provided by these witnesses. It may be that the Prosecution will have to go through the hostile witness procedure with some of these witnesses. If it does, there are consequences to using such a procedure. The potential use of evidence provided by such witnesses cannot have the same weight and cannot be evaluated in the same way as a witness who testifies without going through this procedure. What I'd like to mention at this time is why is it that the Prosecution knows that some of these witnesses might come and go, to use the exact words of my colleagues? I'd like to show you a couple of examples simply of how these people are being interviewed when they meet the Prosecution. Let me go through one example that you have on your screen. That's Witness 142, and this is what we see: "I'm going to ask you questions about the killing and about organisation for killings of many thousands of men but I want you to understand some things. We have part of witnesses to the killing. We have survivors who were part of the execution, who were shot at. We have aerial images. We have seized records from the Zvornik Brigade. We've had many people from those brigades and Drina Corps interviewed. We have your MP logs. What I want you to understand is that it's very important for you to tell the truth. If you try and hide what happened or hide your part in what happened, or your knowledge of what happened, I can prove that you're lying, and I want you to understand this, that this is your chance to tell me the truth right here and now." I let the Trial Chamber read the rest of this interview. And, of course, I'd like -- where he concludes: "I'd like to give you the opportunity of telling me what happened, remembering that I have all those things, all that knowledge. We even have your vehicle logs. Now, can you tell me what you know to have happened." Let's try to imagine for a minute how a witness, whether he was involved or not, whether he saw something or not, whether he learned something by a member of his family or a neighbour, how he feels after an interview like this and how he will feel when he will appear before Your Honours to testify. Let's look at another example. This is Witness 125. The witness says, and I go to the part in bold: "Because at my first interview it was my first time, I was not aware fully of what this regards, and also there have been some pressures on my during my first interview so many things have been left unsaid or incomplete. Quite a lot of things will repeat themselves." And then it goes on. The investigator says: "I'll explain my position now. When you were interviewed, it was put to you that you had some knowledge of the execution. Not that you were directly responsible, but that you had knowledge of them, that some of your assets assisted in taking the men to the dump. We have vehicle records that show vehicles, effectively going from where the prisoners were held to where the prisoners were executed. And that's not to say that you executed those men. That's to say that your troops participated in that and I believe and we believe you had knowledge of that." Again, how does a witness behave, what does a witness feel when he goes to an interview like that? In some cases, witnesses were pressured as suspects, in some cases they were not. But we will see how the Prosecution tried to obtain the evidence. And this, Mr. President, we tell you, will be an important factor in assessing whether these people, these witnesses, how they will react before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, could you please confirm whether when you said Witness number 125 or previously Witness number 140, whether these are witnesses or prospective witnesses in this trial or whether they were witnesses in some other trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are witnesses that are scheduled on the Prosecution's list of expected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. For this trial. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I had two more examples I wanted to show you. Maybe we can quickly go through the next one just to show -- not this one, another one. Next one. Okay. This one. If I can go just before we see where we have number 132, and where the investigator says: "But if you're not telling me the truth and if you're not telling me exactly where you went and what you saw, it's difficult for me to believe that you weren't further involved, that you weren't deeper involved. I'll ask you again: Did you go where the bodies were? I'm only asking you if you were there and saw them. Let's be truthful and honest." I'll leave it at that and move on to my next issue, which is that of, as we hear these witnesses, there are things that we will have to be very careful, potential traps to be avoided. And as the Defence for Drago Nikolic, we will try to do our best to ensure that we avoid these traps. And those include opinion evidence, hearsay, and witnesses being led. All these things in some form are admissible before the International Tribunal. It's a Tribunal that is different from many others in this respect. However, whether it is for hearsay, whether it is for opinion evidence - I'm talking opinion of an ordinary witness and not of an expert witness - or whether it is a procedure in leading a witness, there are procedures established in the case law of this Tribunal, and the Defence will do its best to assist the Trial Chamber in ensuring that these procedures are respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I personally, where I come from, I'm a fan of guilty pleas. They are a good way to administer justice in many respects. However, in this case, where we have a multiple-accused case, I'm really not convinced any more that accepting guilty pleas in such trials is a very good way to proceed. Simply because - and we will demonstrate this when these witnesses appear before the Trial Chamber - we will demonstrate that they had an interest in pointing fingers at others who were not there, and we will show the inconsistencies, the many inconsistencies and the stories that do not hold the road in their testimony. These witnesses have used the guilty plea to their advantage and they have provided information which the Prosecution was looking for, which the Prosecution needed, and which the Prosecution indeed obtained in exchange for leniency towards sentencing. Evidence in this case will reveal that these witnesses did not tell the truth, and that such evidence cannot be used as evidence -- as reliable evidence in this case. Now, as I end this opening statement, I think you will agree with me, Mr. President, that I -- there is no surprise. There is no tactics. The Prosecution knows exactly what our case will be: What we say did not take place and what we say took place, and what we will be contesting. There is no surprise, no tactic, no strategy. Straghtforward, we will try to look at the evidence as it comes in, and we are confident that at the end, after, the Trial Chamber will be able to conclude that Drago Nikolic is not the man that the Prosecution would like you to believe he is. In conclusion, Mr. President, Honourable Judges, first I'd like to thank you very much for my patience. If I did go through some of the law, it certainly was not to try to tell you what the law is but simply to alert the Trial Chamber to some of the areas of the law that will be critical in this case. You've seen again this young lady, or maybe the old lady. I'm not so sure myself when I look at this image. By the time this trial ends, I believe, Mr. President, that you will see one of the two pictures, and that this picture will be a not guilty verdict concerning Drago Nikolic. And if today, if I have accomplished one thing, of alerting you to look at the evidence from a critical standpoint as it comes in, and not to wait for the Defence case, then I will have accomplished what I set out to do in doing an opening statement at this stage. Mr. President, Honourable Judges, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Thank you. Mr. Gvero, you asked the Trial Chamber to give you the opportunity to address it. Please go ahead. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, distinguished ladies and gentlemen, I feel the need as a human being to make several observations on what are, in my view, blatantly unfounded charges. I wish to reassure those who know me well that they were right to have had and still have faith in me. I wish to tell my students, cadets, and others attending the military schools to whom I transferred knowledge from the humanities that I did that out of profound humane convictions without even a trace of hypocrisy or double standards. I believed then and I firmly believe now that our system of values and knowledge was on the highest civilisational level. How one treats them is quite a different matter. I hereby wish to let the Trial Chamber and the public know that I have been and am an honourable man who expresses goodwill towards all ordinary people unburdened by religious and nationalist distinctions, that I have been and am a person who, by his education, occupation, values, convictions, and mind-set finds it unthinkable even to contemplate a crime let alone commit one or participate in one, especially a war crime. No, and no again. Finally, another purpose of this statement is to address all those persons I spoke to through the mass media and who still remember me, judging by the numerous messages of support of late, and tell them that I told the truth in my public statements and that I fought for the truth insofar as the truth was available to me, even though these were difficult times of war when the truth is normally the first casualty and when, under the standards, positive biases are allowed and understandable. Your Honours, when in February, 2005, I learned of the indictment against me, I truly believed it to be an administrative error. When I realised that this was not the case, I immediately decided to appear before this Tribunal on a voluntary basis and I wished for the trial to commence as soon as possible. I didn't even make any particular inquiries as to what the charges were for because I knew that nothing they contained could be true, that I didn't do anything unlawful, dishonourable and inhuman. I was only apprehensive of false testimonies and dishonourable manipulations which were mentioned here today. A popular saying in my people says, two persons without a soul may cost a third person his life. I have been and am still reassuring myself that this Tribunal will not allow this. On my prompt arrival in The Hague, I had time to read various material and to bring back memories about the events that transpired. The material led me to conclude with certitude that I was accused of a crime that I did not even contemplate let alone commit, and which took place in a place I had never been to. I stand accused of being part of a criminal enterprise with persons I had never known or who I never set eyes on in passing and only some of whom I used to meet in the course of professional duty. I stand accused of having been a member of a criminal enterprise together with those persons who I had been permanently in conflict with ever since the start of the unfortunate war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believed that the trial would not take long and that my innocence would be proven quickly and easily. That was why I was extremely disappointed when I saw the joinder of the indictments, because this meant that the trial would take longer and that the decision about my innocence would be deferred. As for the indictment which has an evident shortage of arguments and excess of will to accuse me, even on a stretched and uncertain basis, I want to share only some thoughts of mine. I didn't think I would ever speak about this in public and I feel like I'm in a sort of a confession booth. All that I will discuss here can be found in the material which this Tribunal possesses about myself, others, and the events. I'm nearly 70 years old. When I was 13 I left my home town of Mrkonjic Grad, never to live there permanently again. And never to live, in fact, in Bosnia and Herzegovina itself except for occasional visits. First, I came to Banja Luka without any means whatsoever. I spent the first night in a park in front of the monument to the Krajina tribune Petar Kocic. For about 100 times that night, I read the following inscription on the monument: "Whoever sincerely and passionately cherishes the truth, freedom and homeland is free and fearless like God and despised and hungry like a dog." At that point I swore that I would cherish the truth, freedom and homeland above all else all my life. This became my firm life motto which I believe I have adhered to all my life. I also wish to state the following in reference to the indictment: Apart from the initial officers duty of a platoon commander, I had never held a commanding duty, nor did I wish to do. After the military academy, I also graduated from the political sciences on the integrational processes in the modern world. Therefore my preoccupation focus of interest was the people values and not separation or any such processes. After the studies, I taught humanities in military schools and was a principal of a military high school which prepared young people of all ethnicities to become officers. I was assistant for moral guidance at the corps in Titograd and in the centre for graduate military schools, and I spent several years carrying out moral guidance duties at the SSNO. The Brotherhood Unity Military High School in Belgrade was officially the best in Yugoslavia, and for that I received an award. Brotherhood and unity is the Yugoslav term for some sort of a melting pot, a concept of bringing together nations and ethnicities. I was awarded a medal bearing the same name for my achievements in that process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down a little bit because you're rendering the interpreters' life difficult. Thank you. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Honourable Judges, when I came to the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, armed confrontations were already quite advanced there. I believed that I could give even a small contribution aimed at speedy termination of these conflicts, at least before the fascist spectre and ideas from the recent past were resurrected again. And previously they had produced a lot of casualties. As a result of that, in all negotiations with the opposing side, I readily and convincingly proposed cessation of armed confrontation and conclusion of peace, honourable peace. I knew very well that it was the military who created conditions and the politics who decided on war and peace. I have stubbornly been reiterating my position that the Serbian nation and army in Bosnia-Herzegovina was not -- were not fighting against any nation but, rather, against ideologies and their blinded followers against -- who were against the Serbian people. In your material you have plenty of documents supporting this position of mine. Throughout the war, in the most difficult situations, I did my utmost to act in accordance with my life motto and to preserve, to the extent possible, personal integrity and my own view of events. And I think that I was successful in that. However, many persons of power and influence attempted to exclude me from the public life and even compromised me publicly. In your material, gentlemen, I learned that an attempt on my life was being prepared by those who I now stand accused together with for being in a joint criminal enterprise. It is up to you to decide. I wish to tell you that for the duration of four or five years of war, I never once received a special or fast-track promotion. I did not receive an apartment or any other material gain. I came out of the war poorer than I was when the war started. Your Honours, my entire activity in the war was directed at our army and its people. This was my essential involvement. All my other activities were subordinated to this main activity, including information, legal affairs, religious affairs, contacts with civilians and international representatives and everybody else. Morale is an almost immeasurable category. There are no instruments capable of measuring it, and it is quite variable, especially in combat. The morale of a soldier is affected by how he's dressed to what type of food he receives, what is his security status. The morale of a soldier is affected by what care his family receives, what is the possibility for educating his children, and what is the medical care they receive. Also, lack of weapons and ammunition and success of military and political negotiations, and thousand other things affect morale. People are often quick to judge morale and there are very few of those, even among professionals, who know a lot about it. Your Honours, I wish to clearly state that in this indictment against me, the only true facts are my first name, last name, date and place of birth, my rank and position. It is not true that I was a member any joint criminal enterprise and that I conspired with anyone to commit a crime. It is not true that I instigated anyone to do that or provided direct or indirect assistance. It is not true that I was a perpetrator or co-perpetrator in the commission of a crime and that I was in any way involved in the commission of war crimes. I feel sincere pain for any futile loss of life or every innocent victim, regardless of religious, racial, or national affiliation of victims. I think it is impermissible to speak of victims of one side while keeping silent about the others who fell in the same area at the same time. I think that in the long term, this will not contribute to harmony and cohabitation. But we need to seek the real culprits, which are those who wanted this war, planned it, and who persistently rejected cease-fires and peace negotiations. I did not commit a single crime in war. I literally didn't fire a single bullet or any other type of round. I followed the opening statement of the Prosecutor attentively and I was able to observe that, in relation to the majority of shown documents which are attributed to me, they said that they were truthful, authentic. As a response to that, I have to wonder: Is it a crime to tell the truth? Is it a crime to treat representatives of peacekeeping forces frankly and friendly, and is it a crime to try to protect them? By doing so, I incurred the wrath of some of the powerful individuals from the leadership of Republika Srpska. Based on the documents shown to you by the Prosecutor yesterday or the day before yesterday, it emerges clearly that I was prohibited from engaging in that activity and the ultimate result was an absolute ban on any public appearances of mine which ensued later and which are supported by evidence in the possession of the Prosecution. Your Honours, when I was shown the documents on criteria for war crimes, they said that this army had very good lawyers. It wasn't the lawyers who prepared that. It was myself. There were very clear rules and we know later on how they were applied. It was beyond my control. Your Honours, I'm convinced that I'm innocent and it is up to you to make the judgement on innocence or guilt. Please don't take it against me, but it is my position that we shall all be judged by somebody above us and we shall also be judged on how we judge the others. Your Honours, my defence in this trial will be based on the following principle: I do not wish to shift the blame for my acts on anyone else. Similarly, I do not wish to take responsibility for the acts of others. I expect from this Trial Chamber a just and fair trial and a just decision. Nothing more and nothing else. Your Honours, thank you for listening to me. I have concluded my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Gvero. You may sit down. So I informed you earlier on that there was one remaining issue that I wish to discuss very briefly with you. It will only engage us for a couple of minutes because I am pretty sure that we already have the framework of cooperation in place and that you will only have to act on what I'm going to say. We now have - and I thank both parties for this - an updated Prosecution witness/exhibit list, and as per our guidelines, also a joint Defence notice of the estimated cross-examination time required by each of the co-accused for the witnesses scheduled for the week of 21st of August. Please don't misread me, I'm not criticising either party, but when I look at the Prosecution witness/exhibit list, I notice that the first witness, Witness number 38, scheduled to start tomorrow, you anticipate to examine him in chief for about two and a half hours, but then we have an indication that the following day we start immediately with Witness number 41, for whom you are asking three hours examination-in-chief. Now, the meantime, the Defence position has been communicated to us and to you, and it transpires that with the first witness it's the intention of the Defence to request three hours 30 minutes. With the second witness, it's their intention to request four hours, particularly because there is one Defence team that requires twice as much as any of the other, which we are going to honour for the time being because that's the agreement that we have. However, the thing is that on the short haul like this week, okay, I mean, we are there because you can still say, if you require two and a half hours for the first witness, then the Defence teams can start on -- start tomorrow after you finish with your in-chief, and then, however, they will continue on Friday, and that would practically mean that there will be very little time left, if at all, to have the second witness come on Friday and commence his or her testimony, not to give an idea of whether we are talking of a male or a female here. I think you already got the gist of my message. I think we have decided, agreed to experiment to see how this works. I think it has every indication that it should work well, but take this as one instance which would prompt you to coordinate somewhat better and closer so that the plan for the arrival of witnesses and the commencement of their testimonies is prepared somewhat better. This is the problem. I think I have made myself understood. The reason is that you will understand with us that we have a responsibility to try and economise as much as we can on the resources of this Tribunal, and if it is not necessary to have a witness come two, three, four days before, we'll try and cooperate together to avoid that happening. I understand that this should not present you with any particular problems. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I understand what you're saying. The good news is that, as you know, we are on schedule. All of us have, so far, done well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you're correct, we have been a bit ambitious or optimistic if you start adding up the witness time. We just got their estimates yesterday. When I did this witness before I was on the SALT principle, the first witness was able to do it quicker than two and a half hours, and I've challenged my colleague to try to do it in less than two and a half hours, but as you know, the first witness, he wants to give, naturally, some leeway. Same thing for the second witness. So we will try to coordinate it, but if I could say one thing on a continuing issue, I think, as you know, we agree with the programme of providing material for cross-examination. And I believe you left the issue of how long Defence counsel take on cross up to them at this point. I would like to, as a guiding principle, look to the one-to-one ratio which other Chambers have done with, of course, the flexibility of going beyond that in the appropriate scenario. If Mr. Nicholls takes two hours on a crime base witness, then it would be appropriate to take two hours on the Defence, not three and a half for a crime base witness that through every step of his way is corroborated. Mr. Bourgon is correct: Victims like this sometimes exaggerate, sometimes they will say the enclave was not demilitarised, and this will be brought out very clearly and concisely by either in the direct or in the cross, but an hour and a half extra? I know you'll look to that and you'll make the right decision, because these issues are not contested. They really are not, and they won't be and we'll probably agree with the Defence on most issues of exaggeration or demilitarisation, so if -- that's all I wanted to say on that point. One other reminder before I don't forget, I've heard two accounts of where accused -- I think General Gvero said he'd never been to Srebrenica. It's part of our case that he was there. If there is an alibi Defence, we could again ask them, as they are obligated to, to provide us with an alibi. Mr. Bourgon said that while his client was in the Zvornik area, it appears he's not going to acknowledge that he was at Orahovac, as he knows our case is. So if there is an alibi out there, which appears there is, I would again ask counsel to provide the alibi. It's a bit late in the day, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is already a decision in place, which we handed down months ago. Of course, at the time the composition was different, but we had established a deadline for the intimation, indication of alibis. So please do take up what has just been mentioned by Mr. McCloskey. Of course, I cannot commit myself to anything because these are matters that need to be discussed collectively before they are decided. But if there are alibis that are coming to the surface or which you intend to bring to the surface now, do come forward with the necessary relative motions and we'll act upon them. The other thing is I want to make it clear that we are extremely appreciative of the cooperation that already exists between the two parties in trying to lay out a proper schedule for the presentation and examination of witnesses. For the time being, we are not looking into whether there should be a one-to-one ratio or whether there should be a one-to-two ratio, or I think the -- I just repeat what we had discussed earlier and incorporated in our guidelines; namely, that for the time being this is being experimented, we are taking the word, the commitment of the Defence teams that they will use profitably the time that they seek for cross-examination. We have no reason to doubt that. And we will just see how it goes. But for the time being, we are not prepared to say with the first witness, three hours 30 minutes is more than sufficient. We'll be able to conclude on that after we have gone through each and every cross-examination that there will be. But we are not surprised at the moment, at least for the time being, that starting with the first witness each Defence team would like to make its presence felt and proceed with some kind of cross-examination. Of course, we will use our powers to control cross-examinations according to the procedural rules that we have and that have been in use in this Tribunal. Is there anything else that you would like to address? Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Very small point: We have some map books that we want to give to the Defence and they got away from us yesterday. So come by and get the map books. We also have them for the Court, but of course, Defence -- I don't think they will object, but I know that they will want to see them first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One final thing before we adjourn. There was one issue that Madam Fauveau had raised some two days ago, I think on Monday. I just want to make sure that the revised amendment has now been provided to your client, at least, because that would basically mean that it has been provided to the others as well. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Mr. President, yes, indeed, we have received the copy in Serbo-Croat on Monday. I passed it on to my client on yesterday morning, and I think that was done also by the other teams. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I thank you so much. If there is no further business to transact, then we adjourn and we will reconvene tomorrow morning with the first witness. The protective measures decision will be handed later on today, but there shouldn't be any problems with the first witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of August, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.54 p.m.,
